meta.title: Indoor search rover — practical BOM
meta.intro: The complete build: one list of everything on the rover including what you already own, each part tied to its position in millimetres and the fastener that holds it, the four-motor torque check, the wiring, the pin map, the build order, and a total. Owned rows are pre-ticked and cost $0; the buy list is only what the rover cannot work without, and every screw on it comes from two kits. Prices observed September 4–5, 2026. Physical validation is still outstanding.
meta.margin_note: Margin = torque available ÷ torque required; acceptance ≥ 1.25 because the running torque is calculated, not measured. With a ~130 g power bank and your C920-class webcam the design sits at ~5.32 kg: 1.5 A misses the ramp by a hair (1.23), so the operating point is 1.7 A with the fan (1.40). Weigh the bank and the webcam; if either is heavier than budgeted, swap to the 50 g ELP camera or feed the Pi from an LM2596 instead. The one measurement that matters most: pull-out torque at 24 rpm, 1.7 A, on the real battery.
meta.not_analysed: Fatigue, buckling, impact, vibration, roller wear, uneven floors and wheel unloading, combined-slip mecanum behaviour, motor and driver thermal equilibrium, battery sag under stall, firmware timing, fastener pull-out in PETG, deck deflection under the turret, servo torque with the camera fitted, motor-bearing radial rating (assumed 28 N — thinnest margin in the design), and radar detection at 300 mm height (Walleye measured floor-level radar as blind; this is a compromise to test). No physical test has been run.

design: Four independently driven 80 mm mecanum wheels on the four owned NEMA 17 steppers, a low 350 × 390 mm 2020 frame, the battery slung under the deck for a low centre of gravity, the Ceres pan/tilt turret at the front carrying your webcam and a thermal array so it can look around and track, and both radars on a 200 mm post at the rear looking forward over the turret. Two short-range ToF sensors guard front and rear. The fifth motor and TB6600 stay spare.

No kit does this. Every mecanum chassis kit on Amazon is built for TT or DC gearmotors; none has a NEMA 17 mount. Steel L-brackets under the rails are the cleanest way to put your steppers on mecanum wheels, and the 5 mm couplers in the wheel set match the 5 mm flatted shaft on your motors.

Power is one LiPo for the motors and servos — your gel-blaster pack to start, through one of your LM2596 bucks for the 6 V servo rail — and a small USB power bank for the Pi, which keeps the computer isolated from motor-bus noise. The bank's mass is the price: with a compact 5,000 mAh unit the drivers must run at 1.7 A with the fan to keep the ramp margin. A 300 g brick does not fit.

Finding people is a four-sensor job, and that is how professional search-and-rescue kit is built: CO2 to narrow the area, thermal to confirm a body, a microphone for voice and knocking, radar for behind obstacles. The rover had only the radar leg. So the pan/tilt turret now carries a thermal array beside the camera — a warm body is unmistakable in 768 pixels, in the dark or in smoke, and thermal-plus-visible on one sweep is the strongest line-of-sight detector on the vehicle. A CO2 sensor rides the radar post for closed rooms, and an I2S microphone listens when the motors are stopped. The Pi runs MobileNet-SSD person detection on the camera at roughly 25 frames per second; fusing that with the thermal blob is the demo.

LD2410C is the primary presence sensor for anyone the camera cannot see: stationary or micro-moving people behind a door or a stud wall, plus breathing. LD2450 adds positions and speeds of moving targets and loses motionless bodies beyond about 2 m; it is not the primary detector for an immobile person. Neither outputs heartbeat measurements — and the 60 GHz breathing/heartbeat modules on the market were skipped: their heart-rate figure benchmarks at a 0.33 correlation against a chest strap, and the owned LD2410C already covers breathing. Start with one radar powered; test the two radar types separately, then together for interference. These sensors are not validated here for finding a motionless person behind concrete, rubble, fire or smoke. No detection must never be interpreted as proof that nobody is present.
power: Pack -> Deans T-plug pigtail -> two 22 AWG branches: shield VMOT (four DRV8825 -> four motors) and LM2596 IN for the servo rail. 22 AWG is rated 7 A against a 4 A burst here. No fuse, by your call — the T-plug is the disconnect, so keep the pack leads short and sleeved.

Power bank -> Pi USB-C. The bank must hold 5 V at 3 A: a 2.4 A bank browns out the moment the camera, thermal array and ESP32 are all drawing. Pi USB-A -> UNO R4 USB-C for logic power and serial. Fallback if the bank misbehaves: an LM2596 trimmed to 5.10 V on GPIO 2/4 and 6.
LM2596 OUT -> PCA9685 V+ terminal. Set to 6.0 V with a multimeter before connecting. Servo current returns through the PCA9685 terminal, never through a USB ground.

Fan -> the shield's 5 V / GND header pins (the R4 passes the Pi's USB 5 V through), 150 mA. Radars -> the ESP32-S3's 5 V pin, also USB pass-through from the Pi. The Pi 4's USB ports share a 1.2 A budget: webcam ~250 mA + ESP32 with both radars ~400 mA + R4 with fan ~300 mA ≈ 950 mA. Inside it, but nothing else goes on the Pi's USB. If the Pi shows the lightning bolt, move the radars to a third LM2596 trimmed to 5.0 V.
Pi -> camera by USB. Pi -> ESP32-S3 by USB-C; the ESP32 bridges both radar UARTs. Radars take 5 V power and 3.3 V UART signalling.
Four VL53L1X share I2C only after XSHUT (GPIO 5, 6, 13, 19) assigns unique addresses at boot. PCA9685 is on the same I2C bus at 0x40.
Single common ground at the shield GND terminal. Never put LiPo voltage on a logic rail.
power_after: Motors at 1.5 A per phase draw about 2 A from the pack at cruise — copper loss dominates, not motion. A 1200 mAh gel-blaster pack gives about 30 minutes of driving; the optional 5200 mAh pack about two hours. Holding current at rest costs the same as moving, so cut ENABLE (D8) when parked; mecanum wheels on a level floor do not roll away.
The owned three-pin switch is not in the load path until its DC rating is read off the body and is at least 10 A.

One star ground at the shield GND terminal. The Pi sits on its own bank and reaches that ground two ways — through the R4's USB cable and through the PCA9685's logic GND pin — so keep the PCA9685 power return heavy and short, or servo current will find the USB cable and corrupt the serial link. That exact fault took down the Ceres rover once.
fit: Frame: two side rails along X with outer faces at Y = ±195; two cross rails along Y butted between them with outer faces at X = ±175. Rails sit at Z 71–91. Eight corner brackets, one top and one bottom at each joint, M5 T-nuts, 3.0 N·m maximum or the slot deforms.

Drive: each steel L-bracket goes inverted under a side rail near its end, foot against the rail underside on two M4 T-nuts, leg hanging down flush with the rail's outer face. The motor bolts to the inboard side of the leg with four M3×6 at 0.8 N·m (aluminium threads — the full 1.1 N·m an M3 can take will strip the flange). Shaft through the leg, coupler on the flat with blue threadlocker, wheel on the coupler. Axle at X = ±125, Z = 40. Motor body bottom at Z = 18.9 mm: that is your ground clearance.

Mecanum handedness: front-left and rear-right take the left-hand wheels, front-right and rear-left the right-hand. Check from above — the rollers on top of each wheel should point toward the chassis centre, forming an X.

Deck: two printed tiles 170 × 350 × 5 on the rail tops, held by the corner kit's M5×8 screws into M5 T-nuts — the screw holes are counterbored so only 3 mm of tile sits under each head and the 8 mm screw still gets 5 mm of T-nut. Every board sits on 10 mm bosses printed into the tile and is held by cable ties through printed slots (the Pi and PCA9685 take M2 screws, their holes being 2.7 mm). Battery cradle hangs under the deck centre on four M3×12 with nuts from the M3 kit — 179 g is nothing for four M3s — with a printed retaining bar and two cable ties instead of a strap; battery bottom at Z 65. R4/shield stack rear-left, Pi rear-right, LM2596 ahead of the R4, PCA9685 beside the Pi, ESP32 rear-centre, power bank centred over the cradle. Turret base at X = +110 on four M3×16. Radar post on two M4×12 into M4 T-nuts in the rear rail, flange and tile counterbored so the 12 mm screw reaches. Thermal array in a printed saddle on the camera clamp. Every screw on the rover comes from the two kits already on the list.
compute: Load cases at the design mass, 80 mm wheels, mecanum roller factor √2, mechanical efficiency 0.85, carpet rolling coefficient 0.12: level cruise, level at 0.3 m/s², strafing, and a 5° carpet ramp at 0.3 m/s². The ramp governs. Available torque is holding torque × (I / 1.7 A) × 0.70, where 0.70 is a conservative low-speed pull-out factor that has not been measured. Full arithmetic, every input tagged measured / allocated / assumed, is in drivetrain.txt; every placement is in assembly.csv.

At 1/8 microstepping, 0.1 m/s is about 637 pulses/s per wheel and 0.3 m/s about 1,910. Custom four-axis firmware on the UNO R4 with a timer interrupt, acceleration limits, shared enable and a communication timeout; GRBL is unsuitable and would not run on the R4 anyway. Motor order at the shield: X = FL, Y = FR, Z = RL, A = RR with the D12/D13 jumpers fitted.

Set DRV8825 current with Vref = 5 × Rsense × I. With 0.100 Ω sense resistors, 1.5 A is 0.75 V; read the actual resistor first. Start at 1.5 A with heatsinks and the fan; 1.7 A is the reserve, not the default.

Before calling it working: caliper every part marked VERIFY before drilling the deck; measure pull-out torque at 24 rpm and 1.5 A on the real battery with a lever arm and the hanging scale; then all four wheel directions raised; loaded forward, reverse, strafe, turn; watchdog stop; temperature after 10 minutes; radar trials one at a time then together; turret tracking with the camera fitted; marked-route obstacle stops. None of these tests has been performed.
build: Caliper every part marked VERIFY: bracket foot and slots, wheel width, coupler length, webcam mass, board hole patterns, Ceres base holes. Adjust the tile files before printing anything.
Print: two deck tiles, battery cradle and retaining bar, radar post and bar, fan bridge, two ToF clips, thermal saddle. PLA is fine. Counterbores as drawn.

Frame: butt the two cross rails between the side rails, outer faces at X ±175 and Y ±195. Eight corner brackets, one top and one bottom per joint, M5 T-nuts, 3.0 N·m. Check square with a tape across both diagonals — equal within 1 mm.

Drive: four steel brackets inverted under the side rails, feet on two M4 T-nuts each at 2.0 N·m, legs flush with the outer faces, axle holes at X ±125. Motors to the legs with the four M3×6 that ship with the brackets, 0.8 N·m, leads inboard. Couplers on the flats with blue threadlocker. Wheels: left-hand at FL and RR, right-hand at FR and RL — from above the top rollers point at the chassis centre.

Shield: MS3 cap under each of the four sockets with the drivers OUT. Drivers in, EN to EN. Jumpers on D12 and D13 of the A header. EN/GND open. Trim each Vref to 0.75 V (1.5 A at 0.100 Ω — read your sense resistor first).
Deck tiles on with M5×8 into the top-slot T-nuts. Cradle under the centre, battery in, bar on, ties through. Boards onto their bosses, ties through the slots. Power bank centred on top.

Turret base on the front tile, M3×16. Camera into the Ceres clamp, thermal saddle on top. Radar post through the rear tile into the rail, bar on, LD2410C at Y +50, LD2450 at Y −50, mic between, SCD41 on the rear face.
LM2596: trim to 6.0 V with a multimeter, unloaded, then wire to PCA9685 V+. Nothing else touches this rail.

Wiring, in this order: motor leads to the four sockets (X = FL, Y = FR, Z = RL, A = RR); pack T-plug pigtail to shield VMOT and LM2596 IN; fan to the shield 5 V header; Pi to R4 by USB, Pi to ESP32 by USB, Pi to webcam by USB; I2C from the Pi to PCA9685, both ToF (with XSHUT lines), SCD41; the thermal array on the second I2C bus; radars to the ESP32 UARTs; mic on I2S. Tie everything down.

Wheels-up test before the floor: each wheel forward and back in turn, then all four. A wheel that hums but does not turn is a stalled driver — check Vref and the MS3 cap. Then the floor: forward, reverse, strafe, spin, stop. Then ten minutes at cruise with a finger on each heatsink.

The torque test: wheels up, lever on one shaft, hanging scale on the lever, drive at 24 rpm and load it until it skips. T = F × arm. Compare with 0.254 N·m. This retires the biggest assumption in the design.

Sensors: one radar powered at a time first, then both, then a person walking, standing, lying behind a door. Thermal and camera on a walking person from 4 m. CO2 in a closed room over ten minutes. Mic with the motors off.
pins: R4 / CNC Shield — X (FL): STEP D2, DIR D5 · Y (FR): STEP D3, DIR D6 · Z (RL): STEP D4, DIR D7 · A (RR): STEP D12, DIR D13 · ENABLE all four: D8 (LOW = on) · fan: shield 5 V / GND header.

Pi I2C-1 (GPIO 2/3): PCA9685 0x40, VL53L1X front and rear (0x29 until re-addressed; XSHUT on GPIO 5 and 6), SCD41 0x62. Pi I2C-3 via dtoverlay i2c-gpio: MLX90640 0x33 alone, so its 1 MHz reads never stall the servo bus.
Pi I2S (GPIO 18 BCLK, 19 LRCLK, 20 DIN): INMP441. Pi USB: R4 (serial + power), ESP32-S3 (serial + power), webcam. Pi power: bank on USB-C.

ESP32-S3: UART1 (GPIO 17/18) ↔ LD2410C TX/RX crossed at 256000 baud; UART2 (GPIO 15/16) ↔ LD2450 crossed at 256000. Both radars 5 V from the devkit's 5 V pin, 3.3 V signalling, nothing metal within 10 mm of the antenna faces.
PCA9685: tilt on ch 0, pan on ch 2, as in the Ceres turret_duet firmware. V+ from LM2596 at 6.0 V, VCC from the Pi 3.3 V, GND to both.
review: Microstepping jumpers sit under the driver sockets — caps, not wires, and they go on before the drivers. I first said Dupont leads would do; you caught it.

Four screw lengths I specified were in no kit on the list: M5×10, M5×20, M4×16 with nyloc, M3×30. Fixed with counterbores in the printed parts so the corner kit's M5×8 and the T-nut kit's M4×12 reach, the cradle and turret moved to M3 from the M3 kit, and the fan to cable ties. Zero purchases added.
When the 5 V buck left the list, the fan and the radars lost their 5 V source. Both now run on USB pass-through from the Pi, with the Pi's 1.2 A USB budget written out above.
Motor lead length has never been documented. The far-corner motor needs about 400 mm to reach the shield; plan to extend with your 22 AWG and crimp Dupont housings.

The design mass crept from 4.84 to 5.41 kg through three honest corrections — brackets at 113 g not 60, a 162 g webcam, the power bank — and failed the ramp at 1.5 A before the 2200 mAh pack brought it back to 5.11 kg. Every gram from here spends margin.

items.note: Four drive wheels, fifth spare. 0.41 N·m holding, 1.7 A, 240 g each, 5 mm flatted shaft.

items.item: SmaringRobot 4× 80 mm mecanum wheels with 5 mm couplings
items.note: Two left-hand, two right-hand. Coupler fits the motor's 5 mm flatted shaft; do not print a hub.

items.item: Anndason 6× steel NEMA 17 L-brackets with screws
items.note: Four used, two spare. 3 mm steel, 113 g each. Base slots are 4.3 mm: M4 T-nuts, not M5.
All four used at full length. Nothing to cut.

items.item: TOCLUX 20× 2020 corner brackets with M5 screws and T-nuts
items.note: Eight for the frame corners; the rest and the 40 M5 T-nuts cover deck and post attachment.

items.item: Bemaka 2020 T-nut kit, M3/M4/M5, with M4×10 and M4×12 screws
items.note: The M4 T-nuts and M4×10 screws hold the motor brackets to the rails.
The CNC Shield V3 stacks on the R4's headers; 5 V logic, same pinout. Custom timer-ISR firmware, not GRBL. Frees up when the Walleye rail retires.

items.item: CNC Shield V3 kit with 4× DRV8825 drivers and heatsinks
items.note: Required, not optional: A4988 fails the ramp case. SIX JUMPERS: D12 and D13 on the A-axis header (gives the fourth wheel its own STEP/DIR — bridging X/Y/Z there clones another wheel instead); MS3 only under each of the four drivers for 1/16 microstepping on DRV8825 (an A4988 needs all three — most tutorials show that, and it is wrong for these). Leave EN/GND OFF so D8 controls enable. Insert each driver with its EN pin on the shield's EN mark — backwards destroys it; the trimpot sits on the opposite side from an A4988. Vref = 5 × Rsense × I. Check the kit includes jumper caps.
One over the drivers on a printed bridge, one spare. Powered from the 5 V buck.
Spare. No fifth axis in this design.

Read the label: mAh, C rating, connector (the pigtails here are Deans T-plug). Needs ≥ 4 A continuous — any C ≥ 4 on 1000 mAh does it. Charge only with a balance charger; if yours is a two-wire wall brick, that is the first thing to replace, not the pack.

items.item: USB power bank for the Pi — compact, ≤ 130 g, 5 V ≥ 3 A output
items.note: WEIGH IT. A 5,000 mAh bank (~130 g) fits the mass budget only with the drivers at 1.7 A and the fan running; a 10,000–20,000 mAh brick (300–400 g) fails the ramp case at every current. Needs a real 3 A output or the Pi throws undervoltage with the camera and thermal array on. Keeps the Pi isolated from motor-bus noise and from a mis-set buck.

items.item: DROK LM2596 adjustable buck converters, pack of 5 (3.2–35 V in, 1.25–34 V out)
items.note: One used, set to 6.0 V for the servos (PCA9685 V+); four spare. SET THE VOLTAGE WITH A MULTIMETER BEFORE CONNECTING — these ship at a random output. A second one trimmed to 5.10 V is the fallback Pi supply if the power bank ever drops out.
Not wired in until its DC rating is read and is ≥ 10 A. Until then the T-plug is the switch.
Camera, radar processing, servo control, interface. Model still unknown — affects the 5 V budget.

items.item: Your USB webcam (C920-class, ~162 g) on the Ceres tilt bracket
items.note: The turret was built for it. Person detection with MobileNet-SSD on the Pi at ~25 fps. If it turns out heavier than 170 g, the ELP board camera (B00KA80N9U, 50 g, $22.49) is the fallback.
Primary presence sensor; sees a motionless person. One on the post, one spare.
x/y of moving targets only. On the post 100 mm from the LD2410C.
One bridges both radar UARTs to the Pi over USB. Two free for WiFi CSI experiments.
Bench setup only. Check it is 3.3 V logic before touching a radar.

The biggest gap in the design. A body is ~10 °C above a room and unmistakable in 768 pixels, in darkness or smoke. Rides beside the camera on the tilt bracket so the turret sweeps thermal and visible together. Cannot see through walls — that stays the radar's job.
Two sensors: front and rear, each in a printed clip on the rail's outer slot. Side sensors were cut for cost — strafe only after the camera has seen that side clear.

items.item: Ceres pan/tilt turret: 2× MG996R-class servos + bracket + 100 × 60 base
items.note: From the farm rover. Bolts to the front deck tile at X +110. Camera on the tilt bracket.
I2C 0x40 from the Pi. Tilt ch 0, pan ch 2, as in turret_duet.ino.

items.item: Fgruh 750-piece M3 screw, nut and washer assortment
items.note: 16× M3×6 motor screws, turret base bolts, buck and fan-bridge screws.

items.item: 645-piece M2 stainless screw, nut and washer set, button head
items.note: Radar, ToF and camera boards have ~2 mm holes that no other kit covers. 16 screws used.
Board retention through printed slots (no standoffs), motor leads under the deck, power branches on top, and two ties hold the battery in its printed cradle bar.
Everything, including the power branches: the wire calc puts 22 AWG at a 7 A limit against a 4 A burst — 18 AWG was comfort, not need. I2C, UART, XSHUT, motor lead extensions.

items.group: Only if the gel-blaster pack falls short
items.item: OVONIC 3S 11.1 V 2200 mAh 50 C LiPo, Deans T-plug
items.note: 179 g, 105 × 33 × 20 mm, 50 C (110 A — far beyond the ~2.5 A this rover draws). About 40–55 minutes of driving per charge at 1.5–1.7 A per phase. Half the mass of the 5200 mAh pack: the 164 g saved is what puts the ramp margin back above 1.25 with the power bank aboard. DEANS T-PLUG, not XT60 — the leads in this group are T-plug to match. Balance lead JST-XH 3S. Your gel-blaster pack still runs the first tests.

items.group: Only if the gel-blaster pack falls short
items.item: SKYRC B6AC Neo balance charger, 60 W AC
items.note: Start at 2.6 A = 0.5 C. Follow the pack's instructions.

items.group: Only if the gel-blaster pack falls short
items.item: 2× T-plug to 4 mm banana charge leads, 14 AWG, 30 cm
items.note: Plugs the OVONIC pack into the SKYRC B6AC Neo's banana outputs. The pack's JST-XH balance lead goes straight into the charger's 3S balance port.

items.group: Only if the gel-blaster pack falls short
items.item: Deans T-plug connectors, 5 pairs with 14 AWG silicone pigtails
items.note: Mates the OVONIC pack. One pigtail on the rover splits into the shield VMOT branch and the LM2596 branch; spares for the gel-blaster pack if it also turns out to be T-plug.

items.group: Only if the gel-blaster pack falls short
items.note: On the balance lead, velcroed to the cradle side.

items.note: Omit if the charger ships with the right cord.
PLA you already have is fine for the deck, cradle, post and clips; PETG only if you have nothing loaded.

items.item: Kingston Canvas Select Plus 64 GB microSD, A1
items.note: Only if your Pi has no card.
Electrical tape works for a hackathon; this is nicer.

items.item: SCD41 CO2 + temperature + humidity module, I2C
items.note: The SAR literature's area-narrowing sensor: a person in a closed room raises CO2 hundreds of ppm above 400 baseline. Slow (minutes) and only meaningful in enclosed spaces. On the rear of the radar post in free air.

items.item: 3× INMP441 I2S microphone modules with Dupont cables
items.note: Voice and knocking, the way rescue listening devices work. One mic gives energy only, no bearing; the other two in the pack could later give a left/right bearing. Stop-and-listen protocol: motors off, three-second capture.
The torque measurement: lever on the shaft, scale on the lever, T = F × arm.
Needed for every VERIFY dimension before drilling the deck. Skip only if you own one.
Vref and buck voltages.
